entries.label: What's one achievement you're particularly proud of, and why? Please provide links to what you have built
entries.value: The one I keep coming back to is ClarityAtlas, the iOS health product I co-founded Open Health Intelligence to build and serve as technical lead for. I built it end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with Supabase on the backend, and the hardest technical piece was estimating sleep without a wearable. I used HealthKit and Core Motion signals such as step count, gait speed, phone-interaction patterns, and movement to infer sleep passively, then built a "Sleep Twins" service that matched users on standardized behavioral features with a weighted distance metric so people could compare their patterns against someone similar rather than against a generic average. We shipped it into a live pilot at Johns Hopkins with 30+ users, got selected for the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps, and received a non-binding indication of roughly $75,000 for about 7 to 8% equity, which we chose not to pursue right away because we wanted the right long-term partners. I'm proud of it because shipping the code was maybe half the work. Recruiting users, pitching President Daniels, and re-explaining why the thing should exist mattered just as much. I don't have public links to share here, but I'm happy to walk through the codebase or demo the app directly.

entries.label: What are your short-term professional goals, and how do you plan to achieve them?
entries.value: Short term, I want to own a substantial, load-bearing piece of a real production system rather than isolated tickets, and specifically one where the software has to survive contact with physical constraints. My closest experience is the machine-learning core of the anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization system I work on at Summer Atlantic Capital, where I built the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI detection service, the repository and CI scaffold, and temporal sequence models over event streams with a learning-to-rank layer on top. What that taught me is that model accuracy is not the goal on its own. An anomaly system that fires too often just creates a second problem, so I spent as much time on prioritization, explanation quality, and documenting failure modes as on the modeling. Amperesand is building hardware and software for grid infrastructure where demand is being driven by AI factories and electrification, and the part I'd want to work on is the software side of that: ingestion, detection, and decision support where a bad alert or a silent failure has real consequences. My plan for getting there is unglamorous. Pick the system with the most real users, build it, instrument it, and change my approach when the data says I was wrong.
